items.actClause: AN ACT to establish a task force on arts and music education in elementary and secondary schools; and providing for the repeal of such provisions upon expiration thereof
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S1148

TITLE OF BILL:  An act to establish a task force on arts and music
education in elementary and secondary schools; and providing for the
repeal of such provisions upon expiration thereof

PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

The purpose of this bill is to establish a task force on arts and
music education in elementary and secondary schools. The purpose of
this task force is to examine the adequacy of the current state
curriculum for arts and music education in elementary and secondary
schools and whether sufficient time is devoted to the instruction of
music and arts.

SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section 1: Establishes a task force on the arts and music education in
the classroom to investigate and advise the Governor and the State
Legislature on the current curriculum relating to music and the arts
and what, if any, steps should be taken to alter such curriculum or
increase the time devoted to such activities.

Section 2: The Task Force shall be comprised of eleven members,
including one representative from the Board of Regents; and one member
appointed respectively by the NYS Council on the Arts, the New York
State School Music Association, the New York State Art Teachers
Association, and the New York State School Boards Association. One
member shall also be appointed respectively by the Temporary President
of the Senate, the Speaker of the Assembly; and four members appointed
by the Governor, all of whom shall have experience in various facets
of education and/or behavioral sciences.

Section 3: No compensation shall be awarded to members of the task
force for their service, but they shall be allowed their actual and
necessary expenses.

Section 4: To the maximum extent feasible, the task force shall be
entitled to request and receive, and shall utilize and be provided
with such facilities, resources, and data of any department, division,
board, bureau, commission, district or agency of the state or any
political subdivision thereof as it may reasonably request to properly
carry out its powers and duties pursuant to this act.

Section 5: The task force has 18 months starting on the effective date
of this act to report its findings and recommendations to the
Governor, Board of Regents, Temporary President of the Senate, Speaker
of the Assembly, and to the minority leaders of both the Senate and
Assembly.

Section 6: This act is effective immediately.

JUSTIFICATION:

Based on data reports from the New York City Department of Education,
art programs diminish as students get older. There are four art
disciplines that schools should focus on when designing their


curriculum. About 90% of elementary school students have access to at
least three of those disciplines, while 50% of middle school and only
about 30% of high school students have the same access available.
These reduced levels of music and art classes and performing music in
the upper grades means less variety for older students, and therefore
fewer reasons or motivations to participate in academic programs.
Current research demonstrates that integrating the arts into general
education throughout the learning process, significantly enhances
students' cognitive, personal, and social abilities. Quality arts
education is central to a complete education-and it is required by
state law.  The arts promote the health and well-being of children,
including academic and personal growth, critical thinking and
analytical skills, and the motivation to stay in school and excel by
encouraging expression, creativity, innovative thinking, and
cooperative learning experiences. A quality arts education is a proven
tool to open doors of opportunity through the development of
analytical and problem-solving skills that are indispensable in the
21st century workforce. Arts in Education programs have long been
valued learning experiences in New York State schools.

Studies also indicate that music and art education can have a profound
effect on students with special needs. They are able to build
confidence, develop social and motor skills, as well as become more
self-aware. The difference art can make in the life of a special needs
child is immeasurable, and for this reason should be championed at
every opportunity.

The task force can look into whether, in a general sense, if schools
are meeting the required arts and music in education standards.
Unfortunately, some schools, due to fiscal constraints, are failing to
meet even the most basic requirements for maintaining music and art
education during school hours. Instead, some schools are beginning to
resort to optional after school art programs and for performing music.
The task force may look into the benefits of providing these music and
arts programs as it relates to enhancing pupil academic performance
and improving pupil social interaction with other students.

PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None.

EFFECTIVE DATE:

This act shall take effect immediately.

A.actClause: AN ACT to establish a report on arts and music education in elementary and secondary schools; and providing for the repeal of such provisions upon expiration thereof
A.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S1148A

 TITLE OF BILL :  An act to establish a report on arts and music
education in elementary and secondary schools; and providing for the
repeal of such provisions upon expiration thereof

 PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL :

To establish a report on arts and music education in elementary and
secondary schools for students and make recommendations on the
curriculum and time spent on arts and music education

 SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS :

Section 1: The NYS Commissioner of Education is required to create a
procedure in which school districts report to the State Education
Department on compliance with current arts instruction requirements
including visual arts, music, dance and theater as required by law and
regulation in elementary and secondary public schools. This is a
onetime requirement so that SED can prepare its report on music and
arts education. The commissioner shall report to the Governor and
Legislature on or before July 1, 2018 regarding the findings.

Section 2: Establishes the effective date.

 JUSTIFICATION :

Based on data reports from the New York City Department of Education,
art programs diminish as students get older. About 90% of elementary
school students have access to at least three of the four art
disciplines (visual arts, music, dance, and theater), while 50% of
middle and only about 30% of high school students have the same access
available. These reduced levels of art in the upper grades means less
variety for older students, and therefore fewer reasons or motivations
to participate in such arts programs and in other school activities in
general.

Current research demonstrates that integrating the arts into general
education throughout the learning process, significantly enhances
students' cognitive, personal, and social abilities. Quality arts
education is central to a complete education and it is required by
state law. The arts promote the health and well-being of children,
including academic and personal growth, critical thinking and
analytical skills, and the motivation to stay in school and excel by
encouraging expression, creativity, innovative thinking, and
cooperative learning experiences. A quality arts education is a proven
tool to open doors of opportunity through the development of
analytical and problem-solving skills that are indispensable in the
21st century workforce.

Arts in Education programs have long been valued learning experiences
in New York State schools. The State's arts and cultural institutions,
including museums, libraries, historical sites, performing arts
companies, and teaching artists are crucial in supporting and
enriching New York's school curriculum. Studies by the Guggenheim
Museum, National Art Education Association, and The Center for Arts
Education have proven that students who are engaged in the arts
develop a more complete understanding of personal identity,
appreciation for culture, and connection with community. Furthermore,
art education creates an environment where excitement, possibility,
discovery, and imagination can thrive.

Studies also indicate that art education can have a profound effect on
students with special needs. They are able to build confidence,
develop social and motor skills, as well as become more self-aware.
The difference art can make in the life of a special needs child is
immeasurable, and for this reason should be championed at every
opportunity.

 PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

New bill.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

None.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This act shall take effect immediately.
